bib.title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2024 (38th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems); arXiv:2405.15793v3

read.skipped: Appendix D qualitative case-study trajectories (about chars 150450-283500: four worked instances with long code dumps) skimmed only for headings; heatmap number blocks (Figs 21-24) not transcribed.

question: How does the design of the interface between an LM agent and the computer (commands, feedback, guardrails, context management) affect the agent's ability to solve software engineering tasks?
hypothesis: LM agents are a new kind of end user; an interface built for their limits (simple compact actions, concise feedback, guardrails) will outperform human-oriented interfaces such as the raw Linux shell.
contributions: Introduce the agent-computer interface (ACI) concept and show that careful ACI design substantially improves LM agent performance without modifying model weights.
Build, evaluate and open-source SWE-agent, a system giving LMs an ACI for real-world software engineering tasks.

method.summary: SWE-agent wraps an LM (ReAct-style thought plus one command per turn) in a custom ACI on top of a Linux shell in Docker: a 100-line file viewer, line-range edit command with flake8 linting guardrail, capped search commands, and history processing that collapses observations older than the last 5. The ACI was designed by manual inspection of trajectories on a few dev instances and a small sweep over window, history and temperature, then evaluated on SWE-bench and HumanEvalFix with ablations.
method.task: repository-level software engineering: resolving GitHub issues (SWE-bench), code debugging (HumanEvalFix)

datasets.name: SWE-bench Lite
datasets.split: test subset; used for ablations and analysis
datasets.source: canonical subset of SWE-bench focused on self-contained functional bug fixes

datasets.name: HumanEvalFix
datasets.size: 164 problems per language (Python, JS, Java reported)
datasets.preprocessing: agent starts in a directory with one buggy file and example tests if available; same config as SWE-bench except language-specific demonstration

other.use: labels failure modes of unresolved trajectories

other.note: tried and dropped as subpar in agent setting; no numbers given

inference.temperature: 0.0 for reported runs (selected by sweep over 0.0 and 0.2)
inference.samples: pass@1 from a single run per configuration for main results; 6 runs for GPT-4 Turbo on Lite in Table 10; sweep used mean of 5 samples
inference.prompting: System prompt (setting, command docs, response format, one command per turn), optional single demonstration trajectory from dev set, instance prompt with issue text and 6 tips; response is DISCUSSION plus one bash command in a code block (JSON and XML formats also tried); malformed output gets an error message, 3 consecutive malformed responses end the episode

parameters.history: observations before the last 5 collapsed to one line ('Old output omitted (N lines)')
parameters.search_result_cap: at most 50 results; over cap, no results shown and agent asked to refine
parameters.linter: flake8 --isolated --select=F821,F822,F831,E111,E112,E113,E999,E902 on the open file; failing edits reverted
parameters.commands: open, goto, scroll_down, scroll_up, search_file, search_dir, find_file, edit n:m ... end_of_edit, create, submit, plus bash

other.harness: InterCode-derived Docker environment; configuration via YAML (prompt templates, command files, history_processor, parse_function, env variables)
other.stop: submit, cost limit, or 3 consecutive format errors (Fig 26; Sec 3 text says all past error messages except the first are omitted)

metrics.definition: instance solved in any of k runs (k up to 6)

limits: ACI was designed manually on a few hand-picked dev trajectories for GPT-4 Turbo; the authors say automating ACI design is future work (App E.3).

Ablations are single runs on Lite (300 instances); the paper's own 6-run std is 0.49 points on Lite, similar in size to some ablation gaps (e.g. 16.3 vs 18.0) while per-instance resolution varies greatly.
Only two LMs (GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus) work in the setting; Llama 3 and DeepSeek Coder were dropped (small context) with no numbers shown.
Cost: SWE-agent is 8-13x more costly than RAG on Lite; $4 cap truncates runs and the paper suspects raising it will not help much.
Scope limited to Python/software engineering; transfer of ACI principles to other domains is untested.
Unsure whether demonstrations teach domain problem solving or only command format (App C).
Results are from 2024 models and SWE-bench numbers have since been far exceeded; the paper's SOTA claims are dated.
